steps.prompt: Which sentence tells you more? What makes the difference?
steps.a: A girl visited a city on a day in a month.
steps.b: Priya visited Chicago on a Saturday in May.
steps.reveal: The second sentence uses proper nouns: names of one particular person, place, day and month. Proper nouns make writing specific, and specific writing is easier to picture.

cards.title: What is a noun?
cards.body: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea: teacher, park, pencil, happiness. If you can put “a”, “the” or “my” in front of it, it’s probably a noun: a teacher, the park, my pencil.

cards.title: Common vs proper
cards.telling: girl · city · river · day · school · dog
cards.showing: Priya · Chicago · the Nile · Saturday · Lincoln Middle School · Biscuit
cards.note: A common noun names any one of a kind. A proper noun names one particular person, place or thing, and it always starts with a capital letter.

cards.title: What gets a capital?
cards.body: Names of people and pets · places (cities, states, countries, rivers, streets, parks) · days, months and holidays · names of buildings, schools, teams and companies · languages and nationalities (English, Mexican) · the word “I”. Seasons don’t: spring, summer.

cards.title: Specific is strong
cards.text:
We went to a big park. → We went to Golden Gate Park.
My dog barked. → Biscuit barked.
cards.note: In essays, proper nouns are evidence: the name of a place, a person or an event shows you know exactly what you’re talking about.

prompts: Which proper noun in your sentences makes the reader picture something most clearly?
What’s one kind of proper noun you sometimes forget to capitalize?
